Blocks on this page that list several calls together are reference listings, not programs: they show the shape of each call rather than a sequence to run. Anything presented as a complete program runs as written. The PostgreSQL and MySQL examples need a server, so they are shown rather than run.

Following Along

Most examples below use a small database of posts and their authors. This builds it:

Everything from here on assumes that file exists in the working directory.

Introduction

A database library usually ties a program to one engine. The calls are named after that engine, the placeholders are spelled its way, and the errors are its own numbers, so moving to another means rewriting every call site.

sql puts the parts that are the same in one place. A statement is written once:

Point the first line at postgres://localhost/app or mysql://localhost/app and the rest runs unchanged. The ? becomes $1 on PostgreSQL because that is what PostgreSQL wants, and stays ? on MySQL because that is what MySQL wants. An insert asking for its new id gets a RETURNING clause on PostgreSQL, because PostgreSQL has no last insert id and the other two do. A duplicate key arrives as UniqueViolation from all three.

What it does not do is pretend the engines are the same. They disagree about auto-incrementing keys, about which functions exist, about a great deal of SQL. sql translates what can be translated and is explicit about the rest.

Connecting

open() takes a connection string and returns a Connection.

The scheme picks the adapter. A string with no scheme at all is taken as a SQLite path, since nothing else it could be. MySQL and MariaDB speak one protocol, so either scheme reaches either server, and the connection is described by the adapter for the server it found.

Options can also be given as a dictionary, which is how anything an adapter accepts beyond the connection string is passed:

or alongside a string, where they are merged over whatever it carried:

A connection should be closed when it is finished with, and a catch block makes that certain even when the work between raises:

A connection belongs to the isolate that opened it and cannot be handed to another. An isolate that needs the database opens its own connection or its own pool.

Querying and Fetching

query() runs a statement and reads its whole result:

A result is iterable, so the common case needs nothing else:

For the shapes that come up constantly there are shorter forms:

exec() is for a statement run for its effect rather than its rows:

And exec_script() runs several statements at once, which is what a schema file is:

Parameters

Values are bound by the engine, never pasted into the statement. That is what makes a value a value rather than a piece of SQL, and it is the whole of the defence against injection.

Write ? for positional parameters:

or :name for named ones, where order stops mattering and a name may be used more than once:

sql rewrites these into whatever the adapter wants: $1 and $2 for PostgreSQL, ?1 and ?2 for SQLite, and ? unchanged for MySQL, which already spells them that way. The scanner knows when a ? or a : is not a placeholder, so none of these are touched:

PostgreSQL uses ? as a JSON operator, so a literal one is written ??:

Never build a statement by joining strings around a value, even when the value looks safe. The two forms above cover every case where a value varies. Where an identifier varies, quote it through the driver rather than interpolating it:

Rows, Columns and Types

A row is a dictionary keyed by column name, which is what lets post.title read the way it does.

Two columns of the same name collapse in a dictionary, which is worth knowing before selecting id from both sides of a join. Aliasing one of them is the fix; tuples() is the escape hatch when it cannot be.

Values correspond like this:

Zuri Database
nil NULL
bool a boolean where the engine has one, otherwise 0 and 1
number an integer where the value is whole, otherwise a float
bigint a 64 bit integer, for values past what a double holds
string text
bytes a blob
date.Date a timestamp
sql.Time a TIME interval, on an engine that has one
sql.Decimal an exact decimal
list, dict JSON

Not every engine has every one of those. PostgreSQL has a real boolean and MySQL does not, so a true written to MySQL comes back as 1. db.supports() answers that sort of question without guessing, and each engine's own section below says where it differs.

An integer too large for a double comes back as a bigint rather than silently rounded:

SQLite stores five things and remembers nothing about intent, so a boolean goes in as 1 and would come back as the number 1. What it does keep is the type each column was declared with, and that is what the adapter reads it back by:

A column with no declared type is an expression, and comes back exactly as it was stored.

Exact decimals

A number is a double, which holds 0.1 only approximately. For money that is not good enough, so sql.Decimal holds a value exactly:

PostgreSQL's numeric, MySQL's DECIMAL, and SQLite's DECIMAL and NUMERIC columns read and write as Decimal. SQLite keeps a decimal as a double, which holds fifteen significant digits exactly, so a decimal column there holds at most fifteen, and table.decimal() refuses a larger precision on SQLite. An aggregate such as sum() has no declared type, and comes back as a number.

The CRUD Helpers

Four calls on a connection write no SQL at all. insert(), update(), delete() and find() take a table name and dictionaries, build the statement for whichever engine is on the other end, and bind every value as a parameter.

They are here because the statements they replace are the ones least worth writing by hand. They are mechanical, they differ between dialects in small ways that only show up in production, and a string built by concatenation is where an injection gets in. Anything harder than a flat list of conditions is still written as SQL, and the two mix freely on the same connection.

Inserting and ids

insert() takes a table and a dictionary, and returns the new row's id:

This is the call that hides the largest difference between the engines. SQLite and MySQL report the id of the row just inserted; PostgreSQL does not, and an insert that wants one has to ask with a RETURNING clause naming the primary key. MariaDB has both and uses RETURNING. insert() does whichever applies, and finds the key by asking the schema rather than assuming it is called id.

Where the key is not the column to return, name it:

Several rows at once

Several rows go in one statement, split so that no single statement binds more parameters than the engine allows:

Every row has to name the same columns. A row naming a different set raises rather than being padded with nulls, because a missing column and a null column mean different things.

Finding rows

find() answers with a ResultSet, count() with a number, and find_one() with the first row as a dictionary:

A find_one() that matches nothing answers nil. That is the answer, not a failure, so nothing is raised for it:

What a filter can say

A condition's value decides what it means. A plain value is equality, a list is IN, an empty list matches nothing, and nil is IS NULL rather than = NULL, which no row ever satisfies.

Several conditions in one dictionary are joined with AND. There is no OR, which is the first thing to write as SQL:

Passing nil as the whole filter matches every row. That has to be asked for rather than happening because a dictionary came out empty, which is what stands between a filter built from user input and an UPDATE with no WHERE.

Ordering, limits and pages

order is a list of column names, each optionally followed by asc or desc, applied in the order given:

limit and offset are whole numbers of rows, and together they are a page. A page past the end is empty rather than an error:

A limit and an offset go into the statement text rather than being bound, because not every engine allows a parameter in either place. That leaves them as the one part of a built statement that is not a parameter, so each is checked before it goes in:

Updating and deleting

update() and delete() return how many rows changed:

They read a filter exactly as find() does, nil included: passing it changes or deletes every row.

Values that are not values

Where a value is not a value, sql.raw() marks a fragment to be used as written:

A Raw is accepted everywhere a column or a value is, which is what makes an aggregate or a subquery reachable without leaving the helpers:

raw() is exactly as dangerous as it sounds. A fragment built from anything a user supplied is a SQL injection. Build them from literals, and keep values in the parameters where they belong.

Inside a transaction

A Transaction carries all of them, and they mean the same thing there. A read inside one sees what that transaction has written and nobody else has committed yet:

A rollback takes those rows with it, the reads included, and a transaction that has already committed refuses them the way it refuses everything else.

Where they stop

These calls cover a flat list of equality conditions and stop there. There is no join, no OR and no expression tree, because SQL is a better language for those than any chain of method calls. A query that wants one is a query() or a fetch_all() on the same connection, next to the helpers rather than instead of them.

Transactions

The closure form commits when the body returns and rolls back when it raises, and there is no path through it that leaves a transaction open:

A failure undoes the whole thing:

A transaction() called inside another becomes a savepoint, so a helper that opens one works the same whether it was called on its own or from inside a larger piece of work. Only the outermost commits, and a failure inside undoes just that inner piece:

Schema changes are part of the transaction on SQLite and PostgreSQL, so a set of create table statements that fails half way leaves nothing behind. MySQL and MariaDB commit the open transaction at every create, alter and drop, and a transaction() whose body changes the schema there raises TransactionError when it comes to commit. db.supports('transactional_ddl') tells the two apart, so a program that migrates its own schema can run each change inside a transaction where that holds and on its own where it does not.

An isolation level can be asked for. Where an engine cannot provide one it says so rather than quietly giving something weaker:
sql.READ_UNCOMMITTED MySQL honours it; PostgreSQL accepts it and gives read committed
sql.READ_COMMITTED everywhere
sql.REPEATABLE_READ everywhere, and MySQL's default
sql.SERIALIZABLE everywhere

begin() opens one to be committed or rolled back by hand, for a transaction whose lifetime is not a block. The closure form is safer and should be preferred.

Streaming Large Results

query() builds the whole result in memory, which is right for the hundreds of rows most queries return and wrong for the millions some do. stream() reads the same result a row at a time:

Running to the end closes the cursor. A loop that stops early does not, so anything that might break has to close it:

take(n) reads a batch at a time, for work that batches naturally:

On PostgreSQL this is a server-side portal and on MySQL a server-side cursor, both fetched in batches that { batch: n } sizes. On SQLite it is the engine's own behaviour: rows are computed as they are asked for, so nothing is held but the current one.

A server-side cursor holds its connection while it is open, since the server is part way through answering. Running another statement on that connection before the cursor is read to the end or closed raises rather than letting the exchange fall out of step.

Prepared Statements

Compiling a statement is the expensive half of running one, and a statement run in a loop should pay for it once:

The placeholders are translated once, when the statement is prepared, so the loop does no string work at all. A prepared statement carries the same query and fetch methods a connection does.

A prepared statement belongs to the connection that prepared it. Closing the connection closes the statement too, along with any cursor still open on it, and using either afterwards raises ClosedError.

Connection Pools

Opening a connection is expensive: for PostgreSQL and MySQL it is a TCP connection, a TLS handshake and an authentication exchange before the first statement runs. A server that opened one per request would spend most of its time connecting.

Used that way the pool takes a connection, runs the statement and gives it back. Where several statements have to run on the same connection, which a transaction requires, with_connection() holds one and releases it whatever happens:

transaction() on the pool does the same in one call.

Setting
max most connections to open. Ten by default
min how many to open up front. None by default
idle_timeout how long an idle connection is kept
max_lifetime how long any connection is kept before being replaced
validate_on_acquire check a connection is alive before lending it
on_connect run something on each new connection

A pool wants to be as small as the work allows. Connections are not free at the other end either, and a pool larger than the database can usefully serve turns a queue in the application into a queue in the database, where it is harder to see.

A pool belongs to the isolate that made it, which has two consequences. An isolate that needs database access makes its own. And there is no waiting when a pool is empty: nothing else can release a connection while the call is running, so running out is reported rather than waited on.

Errors

Every error is a sql.SqlError. Catch that to catch anything a database can do; the subclasses separate what is worth handling differently.

The classes are the same on every engine, which is the point. A unique constraint is SQLSTATE 23505 on PostgreSQL, error number 1062 on MySQL, and extended result code 2067 on SQLite; no one of those means anything to the others, and code matching on any of them would stop working the moment the adapter changed.

The engine's own account is kept rather than thrown away. code holds what the engine said, sqlstate the five character code where there is one, and query the statement that failed:

SerializationError and DeadlockError are the two worth retrying: both mean the engine gave up on a transaction to keep its promises, and running the whole transaction again usually succeeds.

Schema Introspection

db.schema answers questions about what is in the database. The queries underneath are entirely different per engine, and the answers are the same shape.

Every method takes an optional schema to look in. PostgreSQL has schemas inside a database and resolves the default through search_path; MySQL calls a database a schema and has no layer above it, so naming one there names a database; SQLite has neither and ignores the argument.

Each column is described the same way whichever engine answered:

indexes() and foreign_keys() describe the rest:

This is also what makes insert() portable: on an engine with no last insert id the insert needs a RETURNING clause, and the column to return is the table's primary key, which is asked for here.

One caution when moving a schema between engines: MySQL parses a column level references clause and then ignores it, so a foreign key declared that way exists on the other two and not there. Declared at table level it exists on all three.

Changing what is there, creating, altering and dropping tables described once for every engine, is Changing the Schema.

Switching Databases

The claim this module makes is that a program moves between engines by changing its connection string. Here is that claim, as a program:

The same report() runs against PostgreSQL or MySQL by opening a different connection, and prints the same list.

Three things did have to be written twice, and they are the three that are genuinely different:

  • The connection string, which is the point.
  • An auto-incrementing key, which is not standard SQL. PostgreSQL spells it serial, MySQL auto_increment, SQLite integer primary key.
  • Any SQL only one of them has. sql does not parse or rewrite statements beyond their placeholders, so a PostgreSQL array operator, a MySQL on duplicate key update or a SQLite json_extract stays what it is.

db.supports() is how a program asks rather than assumes:

SQLite Specifics

db.native() reaches the adapter underneath, where the engine's own features live.

A SQLite database is a file, and :memory: is one that is not. An in-memory database belongs to the connection that opened it, so a second connection to :memory: is a second, empty database rather than another handle on the same data.

Foreign keys are enforced. SQLite leaves them unenforced by default, per connection, for compatibility with databases written before it had them; a database that declares them almost certainly means them, so the adapter turns them on. Pass foreign_keys: false to turn them back off.

SQLite has no timestamp type, so a date.Date is kept as ISO 8601 text, written in UTC whatever offset it carried. Text in that one form sorts and compares in time order, which is what makes order by and < on such a column agree with the clock. A date reads back as the same moment, in UTC.

Functions written in Zuri

A function registered on a connection runs inside the engine, once per row, and can be used anywhere an expression can:

An aggregate is written as a fold: step is called once per row with the accumulator and the row's arguments and returns the next accumulator, and finish turns the last accumulator into the group's value.

A collation is an ordering for text, reached with collate:

A function must not touch the connection it was registered on. SQLite is in the middle of a statement when it calls, and reentering would deadlock. An error raised inside one is carried out and re-raised with its own class intact once the statement has finished.

Blobs, backups and hooks

A large value read with a select arrives all at once. A blob handle opens one cell and reads windows of it:

The cell has to exist and already be the right size: SQLite cannot grow a blob this way, which is what inserting zeroblob(n) is for.

Copying the file with the filesystem is only safe when nothing is writing. SQLite's own backup copies page by page and notices when the source changes underneath:

And the hooks report what the engine is doing:

PostgreSQL Specifics

The adapter speaks version 3 of the wire protocol, over TCP or over a unix domain socket, optionally under TLS.

A host beginning with a slash is a socket directory, which is how libpq spells it, and the socket inside is named after the port: /var/run/postgresql with port 5432 means /var/run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432. A path that already names the socket is taken as given. TLS is neither offered nor wanted over a socket, since nothing sits in between, so sslmode is ignored there.

sslmode chooses how TLS is used: disable never, prefer when the server offers it, and require always, failing when the server refuses. Only require verifies who is on the other end.

Statements go through the extended protocol, which compiles them on the server and binds values rather than substituting them. Values travel in the server's own binary form wherever the adapter has a codec for the type, and as text otherwise, so a type it has never heard of still arrives readable rather than as bytes.

numeric columns arrive as sql.Decimal, arrays as lists, jsonb as dictionaries, and timestamps as date.Date.

Listening for notifications

LISTEN and NOTIFY are PostgreSQL's own publish and subscribe. A connection that has run LISTEN channel receives a message whenever anything anywhere runs NOTIFY channel.

Notifications arrive between other messages, so a connection busy running statements collects them as it goes and poll() hands over whatever has accumulated.

Teaching it a type

A database that defines its own types can teach the adapter about them:

Until it is taught, such a column arrives as text, which is correct if unexciting.

MySQL Specifics

The adapter speaks the client/server protocol directly, over TCP or over a unix domain socket, optionally under TLS, with no client library underneath it. MariaDB speaks the same protocol and the same adapter drives it.

A socket option names a socket, and so does a host beginning with a slash. Unlike PostgreSQL the path names the socket itself rather than the directory holding it:

TLS is neither offered nor wanted there, since nothing sits in between. The connection does count as private, which is what lets caching_sha2_password and sha256_password send the password itself rather than encrypting it to the server's public key.

A statement with no values is sent as text, which is one round trip. A statement with values is prepared, so the values travel in the server's binary encoding instead of being written into the SQL, and the question of quoting never arises. Compiled statements are kept and reused, so a query run in a loop is compiled once.

MySQL keeps ? as it is written, and reports the id of an inserted row rather than returning it, so insert() reads the reported id instead of adding a RETURNING clause. MariaDB differs in two ways that change what the layer above generates: it has RETURNING, and it has no JSON type. The server decides which applies, whatever the scheme: a MariaDB server reached through mysql:// reports db.driver_name() as 'mariadb' and db.supports('json') as false.

What arrives from where

DECIMAL columns arrive as sql.Decimal, JSON as lists and dictionaries, DATE and DATETIME and TIMESTAMP as date.Date, and TIME as sql.Time.

MySQL has no boolean. BOOLEAN is another name for TINYINT(1), so a value written as true comes back as 1, and db.supports('booleans') is false to say so.

BLOB and TEXT share a type on the wire and are told apart only by the column's collation, which the adapter reads: a binary column arrives as bytes and a text one as a string. BIT and GEOMETRY arrive as bytes, having no shape Zuri could represent without inventing one. SET arrives as the comma separated text the server stores rather than as a list, because a list written back would be encoded as JSON and the column would quietly stop matching.

A date MySQL considers absent is written as zeros, and 0000-00-00 is not a date any calendar has. It arrives as nil.

A TIME is a span, not a clock

A TIME column runs from -838:59:59.999999 to 838:59:59.999999. It is a duration rather than a point in the day, so it can be negative and can exceed twenty four hours, and neither of those would survive being read into a date.Date. sql.Time holds it:

Time zones

A DATETIME carries no zone, and a TIMESTAMP is converted to and from whatever zone the session is in. So the session's zone decides what a timestamp means, and leaving it to the server's configuration would make the same database read differently from two machines.

The adapter sets the session to UTC when it connects. Every timestamp then arrives as UTC, and a date.Date written back is converted from whatever offset it carries. To leave the server's own setting alone, pass time_zone as nil, or name a zone to use instead:

Authentication

caching_sha2_password, which is the default from MySQL 8.0 onwards, mysql_native_password, sha256_password, mysql_clear_password, and MariaDB's client_ed25519.

Two of those need the password itself rather than a proof of it, the first time an account authenticates. Over TLS the password is sent as it is. Over a plain connection it is encrypted to a public key the server hands over first, so it is never readable in transit. mysql_clear_password has no such fallback and is refused outright on a connection that is not private, since it sends the password with nothing protecting it.

TLS

sslmode chooses how TLS is used:

Mode Meaning
disable Never.
prefer When the server offers it, without checking who the server is. The default.
require Always, without checking who the server is.
verify Always, checking the server's certificate and host name.

MySQL's own spellings are accepted too. DISABLED, PREFERRED and REQUIRED mean what they say, and both VERIFY_CA and VERIFY_IDENTITY become verify. That makes VERIFY_CA stricter here than on the command line, where it checks the certificate but not the name: the difference can only cause a connection to be refused, never one to be wrongly trusted.

ssl_ca names a certificate authority to trust, and ssl_cert with ssl_key present a client certificate.

Compression

The protocol can compress everything after the handshake:

It is worth it for large results over a slow link and costs more than it saves on a local socket, so it is off unless asked for. A packet too small to benefit is sent uncompressed regardless, which the protocol allows for.

Sending a file

LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE has the server name a file and the client send it. The file is read from the machine the program runs on, chosen by the server, so a hostile or compromised server could ask for anything the process can read. It is refused unless a reader is supplied:

The reader decides what may be sent, which is where that decision belongs. Refusing still answers the server, so the connection stays usable afterwards rather than waiting for a file that will never come.

Statements that answer more than once

A stored procedure sends one result set per select inside it, then an OK packet. query() hands back the first and reads the rest, because leaving them unread would not lose them: it would give them to the next statement, which would then answer with this one's rows.

A routine's body has semicolons in it, and exec_script() splits a script on semicolons. So a create procedure goes through exec() as a single statement rather than through exec_script().

Reaching the adapter

Writing Your Own Adapter

An adapter for another engine implements four things: a Driver that reads a connection string and opens a connection, a DriverConnection that runs statements, a DriverStatement, and a DriverCursor.

Everything above the adapter comes for free: pooling, transactions and savepoints, the CRUD helpers, placeholder translation, cursors, the error hierarchy, and models. What the adapter supplies is the engine.

Schema changes and migrations need one thing more: the engine's spelling of a table. An adapter supplies it by subclassing sql.DdlAdapter, which already writes standard SQL, overriding what the engine says differently, type_name() for each column type and key_definition() for an id() among them, and returning an instance from its driver's ddl(). A driver with none refuses schema changes with NotSupportedError.

The base classes raise NotImplementedError for anything left out, so an unfinished adapter fails where the gap is. An engine that genuinely cannot do something raises NotSupportedError instead, which reads differently on purpose: the first is an unfinished adapter, the second is an honest limit.

What the Module Refuses

Rows are dictionaries. The connection hands back rows, never objects. Models are sql.model, built on top and loaded only by a program that uses them.

It does not write your joins. The CRUD helpers cover a flat list of equality conditions, and models their own columns and associations. Anything past that is SQL.

It does not translate SQL. Placeholders are rewritten. Statements are not parsed, and a function only one engine has stays a function only one engine has.

It does not hide a difference by guessing. Where an engine cannot do what was asked, the answer is NotSupportedError naming the adapter and the feature, rather than an approximation nobody asked for.

Module Reference

The standard library reference documents every class and method. The shape of the module:
sql.open(dsn, options) opens a connection
sql.pool(dsn, options) opens a pool of them
sql.register(driver) adds an adapter
sql.drivers() what is registered
sql.raw(fragment) marks SQL to be used as written
sql.Decimal(text) an exact decimal
sql.time(h, m, s) a signed span, as a TIME column holds one
sql.parse_time(text) the same, read from text
sql.blueprint a table described once for every engine
sql.migrate versioned schema changes, and Migrator to apply them
sql.model models: Model, Query and the errors they raise

On a Connection:
query, exec, exec_script run a statement
fetch_one, fetch_all, fetch_value, fetch_column read a result
stream, prepare a cursor, and a compiled statement
insert, insert_many, update, delete, find, find_one, count the four statements that are always the same
transaction, begin, in_transaction transactions
schema introspection, and create_table, alter_table, rename_table, drop_table
model a query over a model's rows
driver, driver_name, capabilities, supports what this engine is
native the adapter underneath
ping, close, is_closed the connection itself

On a Transaction:
query, exec run a statement
fetch_one, fetch_all, fetch_value read a result
insert, insert_many, update, delete, find, find_one, count the same helpers a connection has
schema, model the connection's schema and models, inside the transaction
commit, rollback, is_finished ending it
connection, nested what it is running on, and whether it is a savepoint

17.1 · The Big Modules

Changing the Schema

db.schema reports what is in a database, and it changes it too. A table is described once, in Zuri, on a Blueprint, and the adapter turns the description into its own engine's statements. The same description creates the same table on SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB.

  • Creating a Table
  • Column Types
  • Columns Are Required by default
  • Keys and Indexes
  • Changing a Table
  • Renaming and Dropping
  • How a Change Runs
  • SQLite Builds a Table Again
  • Engine Specific SQL

Creating a Table

create_table() hands its body a Blueprint, and creates the table once the body returns. Written with its type, as below, the body's table is one an editor completes the blueprint's methods on:

Every column method returns the column, and every modifier returns it again, so a column is described in one chain. timestamps() adds created_at and updated_at, each defaulting to the moment a row is inserted.

{ if_not_exists: true } as a third argument leaves a table that is already there exactly as it is, indexes included. It is what a library creating its own table on every start passes.

Column Types

Each type is the same kind of value on every engine, stored the way that engine stores it best:

Method SQLite PostgreSQL MySQL and MariaDB
id() integer primary key autoincrement bigint generated by default as identity bigint auto_increment
integer(name) integer integer int
big_integer(name) bigint bigint bigint
small_integer(name) smallint smallint smallint
float(name) real double precision double
decimal(name, p, s) decimal(p, s) numeric(p, s) decimal(p, s)
string(name, n) varchar(n) varchar(n) varchar(n)
text(name) text text longtext
boolean(name) boolean boolean tinyint(1)
date(name) date date date
datetime(name) datetime timestamp with time zone datetime(6)
time(name) time time time(6)
binary(name) blob bytea longblob
json(name) json jsonb json
uuid(name) char(36) uuid char(36)

string() is 255 characters when no length is given. An id() is never handed out twice, even after the row holding the highest one is deleted. A decimal() on SQLite holds at most fifteen significant digits, the most a double keeps exactly, and a larger precision is refused there with NotSupportedError. references(name, table) is a big integer referring to another table's id(), with its foreign key.

The modifiers:

exact() makes a text column compare byte for byte on every engine: 'Ada' and 'ada' are two values, and so are 'é' and 'e'. SQLite compares that way already; PostgreSQL is given the "C" collation and MySQL and MariaDB utf8mb4_bin, whose default collations treat case, and on MySQL accents, as the same. A column holding a key, where two values differing only in case must not collide, wants it.

Columns Are Required by default

Every column is NOT NULL until nullable() says it may hold nothing. A value a program forgot is then an error the database reports, rather than a null nobody meant to store:

Keys and Indexes

A key or index on one column is a modifier on it. One spanning several columns is declared on the table:

Indexes, unique indexes and foreign keys are named for their table and columns: posts_author_id_index, posts_slug_unique, posts_author_id_foreign. A second argument names one otherwise. Since the name is known, an index is dropped by its columns as readily as by its name. A name past 63 characters, the longest PostgreSQL keeps, is shortened and finished with a hash of the whole, so it stays unique.

Foreign keys are always written as table constraints. MySQL parses a references clause written on a column and then ignores it, so a key declared that way exists on the other engines and not there; declared on the table, it exists on every one.

The actions a foreign key takes when the row it refers to is deleted or has its key changed are 'cascade', 'restrict', 'set null', 'set default' and 'no action', the last being what a key does when it names none.

Changing a Table

alter_table() describes changes on a blueprint and makes them in the order they were described:

A column described in alter_table() is added. change() turns the description into a change to a column that exists: it takes the type, nullability, default and comparison described, whatever it had before, so a column is declared in full, nullable() included where it applies. Its indexes stay as they are.

The rest of what an alteration can say:

Dropping a column drops every index, unique index and key it is part of, on every engine. A required column with no default can only be added to a table with no rows, since there is nothing to fill them with; on a table with rows the engine reports NotNullViolation.

Renaming and Dropping

A renamed table keeps its indexes under the names they had, and foreign keys referring to it follow it. A table another one refers to through a foreign key is refused, on every engine, rather than taking the rows that refer to it along with it:

How a Change Runs

A change made with no transaction open runs as a whole. On SQLite and PostgreSQL that means a transaction of its own, so an alteration whose third step fails leaves the first two undone with it. MySQL and MariaDB commit at every statement that changes a table's definition, whatever transaction is open, so there each statement stands once it has run.

A change made inside a transaction runs in it, as part of it, and is rolled back with it on the engines that can:

SQLite Builds a Table Again

SQLite's ALTER TABLE adds and renames columns and very little else. For anything more, changing a column, adding or dropping a key, dropping a column an index or key uses, the adapter does what SQLite's own documentation lays out: it builds a new table with the changed definition, copies the rows across, drops the old table and renames the new one into its place, then puts back the indexes and triggers and carries over the sequence behind the id(). The new definition is the old one with only the changed parts rewritten, read from the table's own create table text, so whatever else it declared, checks and collations included, comes through as it was.

Dropping the old table deletes from it first, and with foreign keys enforced, that delete runs the on delete of every table referring to it: a rebuild with them on would take every referring row with it. So a rebuild runs only with enforcement switched off, which SQLite allows only outside a transaction. A change made with no transaction open switches it off around itself, and checks every foreign key before it commits; sql.migrate does the same around every migration. A rebuild asked for inside a transaction while foreign keys are on raises NotSupportedError rather than risk the rows:

Engine Specific SQL

A blueprint covers what every engine can do. For a feature only one engine has, a PostgreSQL extension, a partial index, the statement is written as SQL and run where it applies:

Statements run this way are a part of the same change, transaction and all, as the blueprint's.

17.2 · The Big Modules

Migrations

A database's schema changes as the program around it does, and every copy of the database, a developer's, the test suite's, production's, has to make the same changes in the same order. A migration is one such change, kept as a file, applied to each database once and recorded there, so any copy can be brought up to date from wherever it is.

sql.migrate applies them from a program, and zuri migrate from the command line. Both read the same files and keep the same record.

  • Writing a Migration
  • Running Them
  • Batches and Rolling Back
  • What Is Applied
  • How a Migration Runs
  • When One Fails
  • Several Processes at Once
  • Migrating as a Program Starts
  • The Directory

Writing a Migration

A migration is a Zuri file in a directory of them. Its name starts with a version, a run of digits, and says what it does in letters, digits and underscores. zuri migrate new writes one, with the time as its version:

Each name given writes a migration of its own, in the order given, so zuri migrate new create_posts add_slug_to_posts writes two.

It exports up(db), which makes the change, and down(db), which undoes it. db is the Transaction the migration runs in, or the Connection itself where it runs outside one: always on MySQL and MariaDB, and anywhere for a migration that asks to. Its type is Transaction|Connection, and the change is described with db.schema and its blueprint, once, for every engine the program runs against:

With the types written, an editor completes db. with what a transaction and a connection both have, and table. with the blueprint's methods. zuri migrate new writes them in.

A name of the form create_<table> starts the file creating that table, as above; any other name starts it with empty up() and down(). A migration can also move data, with the same calls a connection has:

Running Them

zuri migrate finds the project, the nearest directory above the working directory with a project.toml, and its migrations directory, and the database from --database, or from DATABASE_URL in the environment or in the project's .env:

From a program, Migrator does the same:

Migrator takes directory, migrations by default, and table, the table the record is kept in, zuri_migrations by default. The table is created the first time it is needed.

Batches and Rolling Back

Every migration one run applies shares a batch number. Rolling back with no options undoes the latest batch whole, however many migrations that was, newest first:

Both directions take a limit. steps counts migrations; to names one:

Every migration about to be rolled back is checked before the first one is: each has to have its file, with a down(), or nothing is rolled back at all.

What Is Applied

status() lists every migration, from the files and from the record, with its state:

State Meaning
applied recorded, and the file is as it was when it ran
changed recorded, and the file has changed since it ran
missing recorded, and there is no file for it any more
pending a file the database has not had

A changed migration has already run as it was then, and editing it changes nothing in a database that ran it. The database has what the old file said; a further change goes in a new migration. zuri migrate status says so when it finds one.

How a Migration Runs

Each migration runs in a transaction of its own, together with the row recording it. On SQLite and PostgreSQL, a migration that fails part way leaves nothing behind and is not recorded. MySQL and MariaDB commit at every statement that changes a table's definition: there a migration runs on its own and is recorded once it has finished, and one that fails part way leaves the statements before the failure in place.

On SQLite, foreign key enforcement is switched off while a migration runs, so a change that builds a table again cannot take the rows referring to it along, and every foreign key is checked before the migration commits.

A migration that has to run outside a transaction, as PostgreSQL's create index concurrently does, says so:

When One Fails

A failure stops the run where it is. The migrations before it stay applied, and it and those after it stay pending, ready for the next run once it is fixed:

Several Processes at Once

Two processes migrating one database at the same moment, as two copies of a server starting together do, apply each migration once. On PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB a run holds the engine's own lock, and a second run waits for the first to finish before it looks for pending migrations. On SQLite each migration takes the write lock as it starts. Either way, every migration checks the record again once it holds the lock, so one another process applied meanwhile is passed over.

Migrating as a Program Starts

A program that keeps its own database brings it up to date as it starts. Nyssa, the package repository zuri serve runs, does exactly this:

A migration directory found from __file__ travels with the program wherever it is installed.

The Directory

Every .zu file whose name starts with a version and an underscore is a migration, and they run by version, as numbers, then by name: 9 before 10, and a version two files share is refused. A .zu file whose name starts with _ is not a migration; it holds code several migrations share, which they import as import ._tables. Files that are not Zuri are left alone.

17.3 · The Big Modules

Models

sql deals in rows, and a row is a dictionary. That is the right shape for a report or a script, and the wrong one for the heart of an application, where a post is something with rules: a title it must have, an author it belongs to, a slug that follows from its title. sql.model gives each table a class. Its records save, check and delete themselves, and reach the records they are associated with.

  • A First Model
  • Declaring a Model
  • Records
  • Filling from Input
  • Validation
  • Hooks
  • Queries
  • Associations
  • Transactions
  • Casts
  • Records as Output
  • What It Leaves to You

A First Model

A model is a class extending Model. Its fields are its table's columns:

db.model(Post) starts a query over the model's rows. Records take the connection to use on every call that touches the database: save(db), delete(db). A record never holds a connection of its own, so it saves inside whichever transaction the code saving it opened, and one kept after its connection went back to a pool cannot write through a connection that is now somebody else's.

Declaring a Model

Every field the class declares that does not start with _ is a column of the same name. Everything else about the model goes in a static define(), which is handed a definition to describe it on:

A model's table is its class name in snake case, made plural by the regular rules of English: Post is posts, BlogPost is blog_posts, Category is categories, Address is addresses. A word whose plural is irregular names its table with table().

define() runs once, the first time the model is used, not when its class is declared, so it names models declared after it in the same file. What it describes is checked against the class then: an association with no field to load into, or a cast on a field that is not a column, raises ModelError at that first use. A model's primary key is one column.

Records loaded from the database are built with no arguments, so a model's own @new takes none that are required, and passes attributes on with parent(attributes) when it takes them.

Records

Calling the class builds a record, from a dictionary of attributes when one is given. create() on a query builds one and saves it:

Saving a new record inserts it. Every column still nil is left out of the insert, so the database's default fills it, and those columns are read back: the record holds what was stored. Saving a record that is already stored writes the columns that changed since it was loaded, and nothing at all when none did, so a column another process changed meanwhile is not overwritten by a save of a different one.

A list or dictionary changed in place counts as a change. A deleted record keeps its values, and saving it again inserts it anew. key() is the primary key's value, whatever the column is called.

Filling from Input

fill() assigns attributes from a dictionary, as a form or a request body supplies them, and it assigns only fillable columns: those the model lists with fillable(), or every column but the primary key and the timestamps when it lists none. A key that is not fillable raises ModelError, so a request cannot set a record's key, or a column it was never meant to reach, by sending one more field.

The second argument takes the keys asked for and leaves the rest, which is the form to use with input that carries more than the record should take:

Validation

A model checks itself before every save, with validate chains, with unique checks, and with a validate() of its own. A record that fails is not saved, and save() raises RecordInvalid:

RecordInvalid is a validate.ValidationError, and its errors are the same { field, message } list a form's validation reports, so the code answering a bad form with a 422 answers a bad record the same way. is_valid(db) runs the checks without saving, and errors() returns what the last one found.

A unique check reports a taken value with the other failures. Only a unique index in the database stops two records saved at the same moment from taking the same value, so a unique column keeps one there too.

Hooks

A model overrides any of these methods to run code at that point of a record's life. Each is handed the connection or transaction the record is going through:

Hook Runs
before_validate(db) before the record is checked
validate(errors) as it is checked, to add failures of the model's own
after_validate(db) after it is checked, whatever was found
before_save(db) before it is written, new or not
before_create(db) before a new record is inserted
after_create(db) after it is inserted, with its key
before_update(db) before a stored record's changes are written
after_update(db) after they are written
after_save(db) after it is written, new or not
before_delete(db) before it is deleted
after_delete(db) after it is deleted
after_load() as a record is built from a row

When a model has any of them, saving and deleting run in a transaction, or a savepoint inside one already open, so what a hook writes is undone with the rest when anything fails. A hook raises to stop the save or the delete:

A model's methods share a namespace with the hooks and with every method a record has, so a model does not declare one of the same name for anything else. A field may share a name with any of them.

Queries

db.model(Post) is a Query. Every method that narrows it returns a new query and leaves the one it was called on as it was, so a query is kept and built on in more than one direction:

where() with a dictionary reads as the CRUD helpers' conditions do: a value matches itself, nil matches null, a list matches any of its values, and an empty list matches nothing. Anything else is a fragment of SQL, with ? for each value, bracketed as it is added, so an or inside one stays inside it. Every condition must hold. where_not() excludes, and a row whose column is null is among the rows a value excludes, since null is not equal to anything.

What a query does with what it matches:

A query is iterable: for post in query reads every record. update() and delete() change every matching row in one statement, without building records, so no validation runs and no hook is called; update() sets the updated timestamp unless it is given.

A scope is a reusable piece of a query, declared with scope() and applied with query.scope(name, argument).

Associations

Four kinds of association cover how tables refer to each other:

Declared as Means The key is
belongs_to('author', Author) this record holds another's key author_id here
has_one('profile', Profile) another holds this one's key; at most one author_id there
has_many('posts', Post) others hold this one's key author_id there
belongs_to_many('tags', Tag) a table joins both keys post_id and tag_id in post_tag

Each name is also the field the association loads into, which the class declares. The keys are named for the class name in snake case and _id, and the join table for both class names in alphabetical order; options name them otherwise:

Associations are loaded when asked for. include() loads them along with the records, one query per association however many records there are, and a dotted name reaches what an association loads:

A field holding an association is nil until it is loaded. load() loads one onto a record in hand and returns it; query.load(records, names) loads onto a list of them in one query per association. related() is a query over what an association reaches, to narrow further rather than load whole.

A record placed in a belongs_to field sets the key referring to it when the record holding it is saved, and has to be saved itself first. attach(), detach() and sync() join records through a belongs_to_many association's table, taking records or keys.

Transactions

tx.model(Post) queries inside a transaction, and a record saved with the transaction is saved inside it:

Casts

Most values arrive as the type they were stored as. A cast makes a field the same type on every engine where they differ, as it is read:

Cast The field holds
bool true or false, from a bool, a number, '0', '1', 'true' or 'false'
integer a whole number
number a number
decimal a sql.Decimal
string text
json a list or dictionary, from JSON text or one already decoded
date a date.Date, from one or from ISO 8601 text

MySQL has no boolean and returns 1, and MariaDB keeps JSON as text, so a model running on either casts those columns: cast('published', 'bool'), cast('settings', 'json'). Null stays nil under every cast, and a value that will not convert is left as it was read rather than lost.

Records as Output

to_dict() is a record's columns, but for the ones hidden() names, and every association that has been loaded, as dictionaries in turn. json.encode() writes a record as its to_dict(), so a record handed to a response leaves out a password's hash:

Two records are equal when they are of the same model and hold the same primary key; a record not yet saved equals only itself.

What It Leaves to You

Loading is explicit. An association is loaded by include() or load(), never by reading its field, so a loop over records never turns into a query per record behind the code's back.

Each query builds its own records. Two queries reaching the same row build two records of it, which are == to each other. Nothing is cached between queries, so a record read is what the database held when it was read.

Joins are SQL. Conditions cover a model's own columns, and related() and include() cover associations. A join, a union or a window function is written as SQL and handed to from_sql(), which builds records from whatever it selects.

Tables come from migrations. A model maps a table that exists; Migrations and Changing the Schema are what create and change it.

Chapter 18 · The Big Modules

Mail

The mail module is Zuri's mail stack: the message format, the three protocols that move messages around, and the servers at the far end of two of them. It is written in Zuri from the socket up, and it speaks to real mail servers.

Mail is older than almost everything it runs on, and it shows. A message is text with a header block, defined in 1982 and extended ever since to carry anything that is not ASCII, which by now is most of what people send. Sending one is SMTP. Reading one where it is kept is IMAP. Taking one away is POP3. Three protocols, one format, and a great deal of accumulated history, almost all of which a program should not have to know about.

That is the design. A message is described by what is in it and the module works out the rest: which parts it needs, how they nest, which encoding each header and each body wants, and what has to be escaped so that a line of a single dot in the body does not end the message early. A program says who a message is from and what it says; it does not say Content-Transfer-Encoding.
